quote: This cognitive work is governed by probability theory, of which thermodynamics is a special case. (Statistical mechanics is a special case of statistics.)
content: This is Jaynes’s maximum-entropy program (Jaynes (1957)), stated as though it were the received account. It is a minority one. The mainstream Boltzmannian program grounds statistical mechanics in dynamics and typicality, not in inference, and its proponents argue that the MaxEnt derivation gets the right numbers only because the dynamics cooperate, which the inference story cannot explain (Uffink (1996); Sklar, Physics and Chance, 1993, a book with no DOI). The essay also makes its argument circular. The previous essay defined the Second Law as “inherently Bayesian”; this essay then argues that any mind which forms true beliefs must be Bayesian on pain of violating the Second Law. If the Second Law is a theorem of probability theory, the derivation of Bayes from the Second Law is the derivation of Bayes from Bayes, and the physics is decoration. If the Second Law is instead a fact about dynamics, then the “special case” claim is false. The essay needs one horn for the premise and the other for the conclusion.

quote: In fact, any part of a cognitive process that contributes usefully to truth-finding must have at least a little Bayesian structure—must harmonize with Bayes, at some point or another—must partially conform with the Bayesian flow, however noisily—despite however many disguising bells and whistles— even if this Bayesian structure is only apparent in the context of surrounding processes. Or it couldn’t even help.
content: Each qualifier weakens the thesis until nothing could contradict it. “At least a little,” “at some point,” “however noisily,” “only apparent in the context of surrounding processes”: a thermostat, a photographic plate and natural selection all acquire mutual information with their environment, and on this reading are all Bayesian. That is the objection Bowers & Davis (2012) made against Bayesian cognitive science, that with prior and likelihood unconstrained any behaviour can be fitted, so that “it was Bayes all along” is a just-so story rather than a finding; the Quest for the Hidden Bayes-Structure is a description of the procedure that generates the just-so stories. The strong thesis that would be worth having, that cognition implements Bayesian updating in some mechanistic sense, is a live empirical hypothesis with real difficulties (exact inference is NP-hard; humans violate the axioms systematically, which is the content of Book I), and the essay avoids it by retreating to the weak thesis whenever the strong one is at risk. A claim that is true of a thermostat has not explained the philosophers of language.

quote: How philosophers pondered the nature of words! All the ink spent on the true definitions of words, and the true meaning of definitions, and the true meaning of meaning! What collections of gears and wheels they built, in their explanations! And all along, it was a disguised form of Bayesian inference!
content: The reference is to Book III’s claim that categorization is naive Bayes over a hub-and-spoke network. Book III’s annotations recorded what became of that: the psychological model it formalizes was tested and rejected (Rehder (2003), causal-model theory outperforming feature-similarity and naive-Bayes accounts), and the systems that now actually handle words, meanings and definitions at human level are not Bayesian in mechanism and were not explained by the Bayesians who, Book III predicted, would arrive to explain them. The essay treats a network diagram it drew as the discovery that dissolves two thousand years of philosophy of language, and reports disappointment that the audience did not stand up. The audience had reasons: the diagram was not tested, and the parts of the problem the philosophers were arguing about (reference, externalism, the analytic/synthetic distinction) are not touched by a classifier of any kind, Bayesian or otherwise.

quote: If you can’t see the detailed flow of probability, you have nothing but a password—or, a bit more charitably, a hint at the form an answer would take; but certainly not an answer.
content: By this standard the essay ends with a password. Its closing paragraph offers “the Force underlying all cognition,” “the Bayes-Sight,” and a quotation from Zelazny about seeing “the clear, cold lines of eternity,” and its middle section declines to say where it is going on the ground that the rhythm cannot be conveyed. The essay is honest about this and it is the right standard; the problem is what happens when the standard is applied to the one worked example the essay claims, the Book III account of words, which supplied a diagram rather than a flow. There is a further difficulty for the “Grail always turns out to be the same” programme. The heuristics that Gigerenzer & Brighton (2009) showed outperforming regression and Bayesian models out of sample do so by discarding available cues; the thing that makes them work is the thing that a calculation using “every scrap of available knowledge” cannot do, and calling the discarding a hidden Bayesian structure gives the word a meaning on which it no longer excludes anything. The essay says the Grail must be “the entire Grail, without any parts missing.” Under the bias–variance tradeoff, the parts that are missing are the reason the cup holds water.
